\[
I_{\text{out}} = \frac{255}{n - 1} \min\!\left(n - 1,\ \left\lfloor \frac{n I}{256} \right\rfloor\right),
\qquad n = 4
\]

The formula shows the default parameter values.

where

- \(I\): Input value from 0 to 255
- \(n\): The number of levels

The range 0 to 255 is cut into n bins of equal width 256 / n. Each bin maps to one of n levels spread evenly from 0 to 255, so black and white stay. This bin rule is PixelNexus's own. Programs differ here. Pillow's ImageOps.posterize keeps the top bits of each value instead, and others round to the nearest level. Gonzalez and Woods show the same effect when they reduce the number of intensity levels.
